subtype: Crush × Caste, religion or family barrier [Actor]
passage:
"Irfan, I think I like Neha."
"Neha from the library? Good. So what's the problem?"
"Her family is strict about marrying inside their community. Mine has opinions too."
"Have you told her any of this?"
"No. I keep thinking it will sort itself out if we're happy enough."
"Will it?"
Abhinav laughed, then stopped. "Probably not. Her parents won't care how happy we are."
"So what do you want from her? A few nice months, or a real future?"
"I don't know yet. I should work that out before I ask her anything. And ask what she wants, too."
"And your family?"
"I need a plan for that, not just hope. Maybe I'll start with my sister." 
"Better than hiding it until someone finds out 🙂"

qa.q: What is Neha's family strict about, according to Abhinav?
qa.a: Neha's family is strict about marrying inside their community.

qa.q: What does it suggest that Abhinav laughs and then stops when Irfan asks if things will sort themselves out?
qa.a: It suggests Abhinav realises, mid-laugh, that being happy together probably will not change her parents' minds, so Abhinav's hope was shakier than admitted.

qa.q: What should Abhinav do before he says anything to Neha?
qa.a: Work out honestly what Abhinav wants, ask what she wants, and think through how each family might be approached, instead of trusting that love alone will win.

qa.q: How might Neha feel if the family problem only surfaced suddenly after they had grown close?
qa.a: She might feel blindsided and upset that she was never given the chance to think it through with Abhinav earlier.

grounding: Shows a crush across a family and community barrier where the person thinks about real wants and a plan instead of hoping love wins.

passage:
Rain hammered the tin roof of the bus stop. Yamini had twenty minutes before the portfolio deadline at the design institute, and Vaibhav's folder was still in her bag; he had left it on her desk that morning. Her phone buzzed with a message from friends: "Anniversary pic?? 🎉" She thumbed it away and ran for the auto, holding the folder under her dupatta.

She reached the gate as he was pacing outside. He looked at the folder, then at her, and laughed with relief.

"If you get in, it means Ahmedabad for two years," she said, catching her breath. "I'll be sad. I'll also be proud. Let's figure out calls now, and tell each other honestly if it gets hard."

She posted nothing that day. He'd made the deadline; that felt like enough.

qa.q: Why was Yamini running through the rain?
qa.a: She was bringing Vaibhav the portfolio he had left on her desk, so he could submit it before the deadline at the institute.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling about the possible move to Ahmedabad?
qa.a: Mixed feelings: she says she will be sad but also proud, which shows she wants him to go without hiding her own side of it.

qa.q: What could Yamini and Vaibhav do if he does move for two years?
qa.a: Agree on realistic times for calls, keep telling each other honestly when it gets hard, and plan visits.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see Yamini turning up at the gate with his folder?
qa.a: He probably feels backed by her, and reassured that his ambition is welcome and not something that threatens them.

grounding: Shows commitment expressed through reliability, honest talk and room for a partner's growth rather than a public post.

passage:
Gargi, come sit. Your Neelam Masi was twenty once too, and I want to tell you about Rohan.

He brought me tea at the library every evening. He remembered my exam dates before I did. Nobody had ever fussed over me like that, and I'd glow for an hour and then get a knot in my stomach. What if I couldn't be that person for him?

So one night I said it aloud: "I like you very much, but I'm not ready to promise big things." He went quiet, then nodded, and stayed anyway.

And I kept my Thursday evenings with Shanti and the hostel girls. Once I forgot to thank him for the tea and noticed only when he stopped bringing it for two days. I thanked him properly after that.

qa.q: What did Rohan do at the library every evening?
qa.a: Rohan brought Neelam tea at the library every evening.

qa.q: Why did being chosen feel both warm and frightening to Neelam?
qa.a: It felt warm to be valued so much, but she worried she could not live up to that devotion, which is why she spoke honestly about not being ready.

qa.q: What would you tell someone who has just been chosen with this kind of devotion?
qa.a: Be honest about what you can and cannot promise, keep your own friendships going, and say thank you instead of taking the care for granted.

qa.q: How might Rohan have felt when Neelam said she was not ready to promise big things?
qa.a: He may have been disappointed for a moment, but also relieved to know where she stood instead of guessing.

grounding: Shows the warmth and slight fear of being chosen, met with honesty about limits and keeping one's own friendships.

passage:
Sunil, sit down. Francis Uncle isn't going to lecture you, only tell you what happened with Ankita.

At twenty I had a habit: if she said, "I'll call at nine," I'd watch the clock. And at nine my phone rang. Every time. Little promises, kept. That's how I started believing her without asking for proof.

One evening she went silent for two hours. I felt that itch to check her location, to set some little test. I didn't. She called later, worn out from a lab that ran late.

But I wasn't blind. When she cancelled three Sundays running with vague reasons, I asked her plainly what was going on. She told me about a family worry she'd been carrying alone. Believing her and asking her weren't opposites.

qa.q: When did Ankita's phone call arrive when she promised to call?
qa.a: At nine, exactly as she had said it would.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when Ankita went silent for two hours?
qa.a: He felt an itch to check her location and set some kind of test, which shows he was uneasy, yet he chose to wait.

qa.q: What can someone do when they feel the urge to test a partner?
qa.a: Ask plainly about the specific worry and watch whether small promises keep being kept, instead of setting traps.

qa.q: How would Ankita likely have felt if Francis had secretly checked her location that evening?
qa.a: She would probably have felt watched and distrusted, and might have been less willing to open up about things later.

grounding: Shows trust built through small kept promises, not blind, with a plain question asked when something seemed off.

passage:
By second year, Yusuf was my weather. If his messages were cheerful, I was fine; if they were short, I spent the afternoon rereading them. I asked him which elective to pick, what to wear, even whether to go home for Diwali. I'd quit the dance club because he wasn't there, and weekends without him felt hollow.

"Reena, are you seriously waiting for him to text first again?" my roommate said one Saturday.

I sat there, ashamed, then went to dance practice out of spite. Halfway through a step I caught myself laughing with people who didn't know or care what Yusuf thought. I could still be someone without him in the room. That surprised me, and it made choosing him feel different, lighter.

qa.q: Which questions did Reena ask Yusuf to decide for her?
qa.a: Reena asked him which elective to pick, what to wear, and whether to go home for Diwali.

qa.q: How did Reena feel on weekends without Yusuf, and what shows it?
qa.a: Reena felt lost and empty, since she says the weekends felt hollow and she quit the dance club because he was not there.

qa.q: What step helped Reena, and why might it work?
qa.a: Going back to dance practice helped, because having Reena's own friends and interests means being with Yusuf becomes a choice, not a need.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have felt being the source of all of Reena's moods?
qa.a: He may have felt weighed down, unable to have a short or bad day without worrying it would upset Reena.

grounding: Shows leaning on a partner for mood and decisions, then rebuilding one's own friends and activities so love becomes a choice.

passage:
Anjali's lab practical was at nine the next morning, and her notes lay untouched beside her chai. Her phone buzzed again. Joseph: "Are you free? Everything feels awful. Please pick up 🥺"

That was the fourth call since dinner. She had already missed football practice twice that week to sit with him, and each time he said he didn't know what he'd do without her. She loved him, and still her chest felt tight, and the guilt was worse than the tightness.

She called back. "I care about you, and I can't be your only person tonight. Have you talked to your brother? I'll come on Saturday afternoon, properly, for the whole afternoon."

The line was quiet for a long moment before he said, "Okay."

She went back to her notes, shaky but steady.

qa.q: How many times had Anjali missed football practice that week?
qa.a: She had missed it twice that week.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling as Joseph's messages kept coming?
qa.a: She felt torn: she loved him but also felt heavy and guilty, as her tight chest and untouched notes show.

qa.q: Which part of Anjali's call made it kind rather than cold?
qa.a: She said she cares, named her limit for that night, offered a definite time on Saturday, and pointed him toward his brother.

qa.q: How might Joseph have felt when Anjali said she could not be his only person?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt or rejected at first, but hearing that she still planned to come on Saturday could help him feel less alone.

grounding: Shows a partner's constant need feeling heavy, with care given, a limit named kindly, and another support encouraged.

passage:
Yosef had already priced a flat in Rotterdam when Noa put her fork down.

"The lab in Bergen wrote back," she said. "They want me in September."

His stomach dropped. His own plan had a place for her in it, and that place was Rotterdam. He breathed out slowly. "Tell me about the lab first. What would you actually do there?"

She talked for ten minutes about kelp surveys and a supervisor she admired, and he listened without doing sums in his head. Then he pulled over a napkin. "Two people, two offers. What are our options?"

They wrote them down: he goes, she goes, or a year of visits between the two cities. Nothing was decided. Afterwards he washed the dishes, since she had cooked.

qa.q: Where had Yosef already priced a flat?
qa.a: He had already priced a flat in Rotterdam.

qa.q: How did Yosef feel when Noa mentioned the lab, and why?
qa.a: He felt thrown and anxious, his stomach dropping, because his own plan had a place for her in Rotterdam and he realised he had expected her to adjust.

qa.q: What could Yosef do next so the decision stays shared?
qa.a: Keep asking what each of them wants, compare the options honestly, and agree who adjusts when, so it is not always Noa who moves.

qa.q: How might Noa have felt if Yosef had answered that Rotterdam was better anyway?
qa.a: She might have felt her ambitions counted for less and that she was being asked to follow, not to choose.

grounding: Shows wanting an equal partner: asking about her ambitions, listing options together and splitting effort fairly.

passage:
For a while I kept a little ledger in my head: who paid for dinner, who replied first, who owed whom. I'd sulk when a favour wasn't repaid, though I never said so.

The week my thesis draft was torn apart by my guide, I stopped counting. Samir turned up at ten at night with a tiffin of dal and rice and asked nothing. He sat on my floor proofreading references until past midnight, humming quietly, and didn't leave until they were done.

The next evening I said, "Thank you for the tiffin, and for staying until the references were finished. That was what got me through." I saw his ears go pink.

Two weeks later, when his cousin's engagement had him frazzled, I was the one at his door, with tea. Kunal, I thought, this is the part I wasn't doing.

qa.q: What did Samir bring at ten at night?
qa.a: He brought a tiffin of dal and rice.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt as Samir quietly proofread on the floor?
qa.a: Kunal likely felt grateful and a little uncomfortable, since Samir's help was not something to tally and the old habit of counting favours and sulking suddenly looked petty.

qa.q: What could Kunal do beyond saying thank you?
qa.a: Show up for Samir in his own hard week, as Kunal did with the tea, without expecting a matching favour back.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt on hearing Kunal's specific thanks?
qa.a: He probably felt seen, since he learned exactly which part of his quiet effort mattered, which fits the pink ears.

grounding: Shows noticing a partner's quiet support, thanking specifically and reciprocating instead of scorekeeping.

passage:
Dear Sarika didi,

You asked how things are with Dev. Honestly, I'm tired. I send him "where are you?" texts and then hate myself. I say yes to films I don't like and tell him I'm fine when I'm not.

Last Friday, when he went to wash his hands, I picked up his phone. My thumb was on the screen when I saw my own face reflected in it, and I put it down.

That night I told him the truth: "I get scared you'll leave. It's my fear, not your fault." He held my hand for a long time and didn't make a joke of it.

I've also started a pottery class, only mine. My hands are always muddy and I don't mind it.

Write back soon 🙂

Lavanya

qa.q: What did Lavanya do when Dev went to wash his hands?
qa.a: Lavanya picked up Dev's phone but put it down on seeing Lavanya's own face reflected in the screen.

qa.q: What might Lavanya be worried about, given that she says yes to films she dislikes and texts him constantly?
qa.a: Lavanya was afraid Dev would leave, which pushed Lavanya to check on him and to please him too much.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do that helped, and what else could Lavanya try?
qa.a: Lavanya told Dev the fear was Lavanya's own and began a class just for Lavanya; next, Lavanya could keep building friendships and self-worth, and go on talking openly with him.

qa.q: How might Dev have felt about the constant texts before Lavanya explained?
qa.a: He may have felt crowded or confused, unsure what he needed to prove, until Lavanya's explanation let him respond with reassurance.

grounding: Shows anxiety about being left, with the person naming the fear and building their own worth instead of checking or testing.

passage:
Vandana sat on the terrace of her house in the small town, phone in hand, watching one grey tick under her message. Arun was in Toronto, half a day behind, and his replies came when she was asleep or in class. This was the third night that week. She began to type, "You clearly don't care," and stared at it.

"Madhuri, look at this," she called down to her friend, who ran the tailoring shop next door.

Madhuri read it and raised an eyebrow. "Do you know his timetable?"

Vandana deleted the line. She wrote instead: "I miss you, and this week I felt left out of your days. Can we fix Sunday 9 pm my time for a proper call? And can we plan a visit when your term ends in December?"

His reply came at dawn: "Yes. Sorry. Yes."

qa.q: In which city is Arun living?
qa.a: Arun is in Toronto.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling as she watched the single grey tick, and what did she nearly do?
qa.a: She felt hurt and left out, and she nearly sent a message saying he clearly did not care before deleting it.

qa.q: What agreement in Vandana's new message could ease the distance?
qa.a: A fixed Sunday call time that suits them both, plus a planned visit when his term ends in December.

qa.q: How might Arun see the silence that upset Vandana?
qa.a: He may have been busy with classes or asleep because of the time difference, so the silence could be about schedules rather than neglect.

grounding: Shows long-distance strain where the person replaces an accusation with an honest message and plans for realistic contact and a visit.
